section_summary: This closing section documents U.S.–Japanese cooperation and diplomatic procedures concerning narcotics enforcement, including the travel and surveillance of suspected traffickers and investigations of morphine smuggled aboard the Heian Maru. It also contains Japanese regulations governing cannabis and other narcotics, reports about suspicious vessels, and allegations that Japanese interests were promoting or protecting the opium traffic in China. The section ends with cross-references, press material, and diplomatic correspondence about opium moving through Japan, Manchukuo, and Japanese-occupied China.

subfiles.title: Treasury letter concerning Anslinger's reply to Mitani
subfiles.from: Stephen B. Gibbons, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Reports that Commissioner Anslinger had already answered Mitani's letter concerning Shinji Taniguchi's visit.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury explains that Mitani's original November 1937 letter reached the Bureau of Narcotics and that Anslinger replied on December 1, 1937. It encloses copies of that reply and promises that future communications with Mitani will be made only under State Department instructions.

subfiles.title: Anslinger letter to T. Mitani
subfiles.from: H. J. Anslinger, Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.to: T. Mitani, Director of the Bureau of Treaties and Conventions
subfiles.about: Thanks Mitani for facilitating Taniguchi's visit and expresses interest in continued cooperation.
subfiles.summary: Anslinger describes his meetings with Taniguchi as useful for exchanging information and planning action against illicit narcotics traffic. He praises Taniguchi's ability and hopes that American officials can visit Japan in the following year.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting Hajime Hoshi's visitor visa
subfiles.from: Cameron, American Consulate General at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the issuance of a temporary visitor visa to Hajime Hoshi and his intended itinerary.
subfiles.summary: Hoshi was expected to arrive at San Francisco aboard the Tatsuta Maru on May 23. He stated that he would later travel from New York to South America.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Anslinger–Mitani correspondence
subfiles.about: Forwards Treasury correspondence concerning Shinji Taniguchi's visit to the United States.
subfiles.summary: The Department refers to the Embassy's November 1937 despatch about Taniguchi and the illicit drug traffic between Japan and the United States. It encloses the Treasury's April 29 letter and Anslinger's December 1 reply to Mitani.

subfiles.title: Confidential notification to Treasury concerning Hajime Hoshi
subfiles.about: Alerts Treasury that suspected trafficker Hajime Hoshi was traveling to San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: The State Department encloses the Tokyo telegram reporting Hoshi's temporary visa. It identifies him as suspected of complicity in illicit narcotics traffic and states that the Tatsuta Maru was due at San Francisco around May 23.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Iranian opium shipped to China
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to telegrams about Iranian opium imported into China under Japanese auspices.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies telegram sections dated May 6, 9, and 13 from M. R. Nicholson, the Treasury representative at Shanghai. Those messages concerned an Iranian opium shipment allegedly operating with Japanese support.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2894 on narcotics-information procedures in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Explains the agreed procedure for urgent narcotics communications between the Embassy, consular officers, Treasury representatives, and Japanese authorities.
subfiles.summary: Grew acknowledges approval of the information-exchange procedure and says Treasury representatives at Kobe and Yokohama may telephone or telegraph the Embassy in urgent cases. Direct contacts with local Japanese authorities remain restricted, while the Embassy will approach the appropriate central officials for immediate action. Grew reports that this system had operated since the previous July without unfavorable results.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of Despatch No. 2894
subfiles.from: Moore, Counselor, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards Grew's report on the working of narcotics-investigation arrangements in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter answers Elmer L. Irey's April 1 communication to Stanley K. Hornbeck. It encloses a copy of Grew's Despatch No. 2894 for Treasury's information.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmittal concerning Hajime Hoshi
subfiles.about: Transmits Customs reports tracing Hajime Hoshi's travel across the United States.
subfiles.summary: Treasury sends three copies each of a May 31 San Francisco letter and a June 22 New York report. Both concern Hoshi, described as a Japanese drug manufacturer.

subfiles.title: San Francisco Customs report on Hajime Hoshi
subfiles.from: D. W. Swift, Customs Agent, approved by J. P. Sheehan
subfiles.to: Supervising Customs Agent at New York
subfiles.about: Reports Hoshi's arrival in San Francisco and departure eastward by way of Los Angeles.
subfiles.summary: Hoshi arrived on May 23 and left San Francisco on May 29, carrying only a few handbags and using a Japanese transfer company. He reportedly intended a short stay in Los Angeles before proceeding to New York and then South America.

subfiles.title: New York Customs report on Hajime Hoshi's departure
subfiles.from: Gerard C. Lundy, Customs Agent, approved by J. W. Roberts
subfiles.about: Reports that Hoshi sailed from New York for Callao and was placed on a Customs information list.
subfiles.summary: Hoshi departed New York on June 17 aboard the Grace Line steamship Santa Barbara, giving Callao, Peru, as his destination. Customs arranged for a thorough search of his baggage and effects if he returned to New York.

subfiles.title: Instruction reporting Hoshi's movements
subfiles.to: American consular officer in charge at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards Treasury reports about Hajime Hoshi's arrival in San Francisco and departure for Peru.
subfiles.summary: The Department recalls the May 5 Tokyo telegram identifying Hoshi as a suspected narcotics trafficker. It encloses the June 24 Treasury letter and its reports tracing his journey from San Francisco to Callao.

subfiles.title: Request for Japanese cannabis laws and regulations
subfiles.about: Renews a request for laws governing the importation of cannabis sativa throughout the Japanese Empire.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that it has received no reply to its September 1937 request for Japanese and territorial cannabis regulations. It asks for the material without further delay so that the United States can meet obligations under the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese complicity in China's opium trade
subfiles.about: Cross-references a memorandum about planned American and British representations to Japan over opium sales in China.
subfiles.summary: The British Ambassador was informed that the United States planned representations concerning Japanese complicity in Chinese opium sales. He promised to report the nature and probable timing of corresponding British representations.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Japanese Geneva communiqué on narcotics in China
subfiles.about: Forwards a communiqué defending Japanese conduct regarding narcotics in occupied parts of China.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends a photostatic copy of a communiqué reportedly issued by the Japanese press or propaganda bureau in Geneva. The communiqué addressed narcotics traffic in Chinese areas then under Japanese control.

subfiles.title: Port-au-Prince report on the Keiyo Maru
subfiles.about: Reports the brief visit and parcel-post activity of a Japanese vessel listed in a narcotics-smuggling memorandum.
subfiles.summary: The Keiyo Maru anchored offshore at Port-au-Prince on October 28 while bound for New Orleans by way of Havana. It discharged seven bags of parcel post and collected six more; one incoming package addressed to the local Director of Public Health could not be opened by Customs.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal of the Keiyo Maru report
subfiles.about: Forwards the Port-au-Prince report and supplies the suspected vessel's published itinerary.
subfiles.summary: The Department identifies the Keiyo Maru as a Japanese motor vessel suspected of illicit narcotics activity and encloses Despatch No. 171. It notes that the Coast Guard likely issued the cited weekly memorandum and reproduces an itinerary including Cebu, Saigon, Tianjin, Kobe, Nagoya, Yokohama, Tacoma, Cristóbal, and New Orleans.

subfiles.title: Letter to Treasury on Ordinance No. 17 and cannabis controls
subfiles.about: Identifies earlier Japanese legal material relevant to cannabis importation and the Marihuana Tax Act.
subfiles.summary: The Department calls Treasury's attention to Ordinance No. 17 of May 19, 1930, and to a 1931 Embassy narcotics questionnaire. It says the Embassy is being asked whether the ordinance remains in effect.

subfiles.title: Inquiry whether Ordinance No. 17 remains in force
subfiles.about: Asks the Embassy to determine whether Japan's 1930 narcotics-import ordinance is still effective.
subfiles.summary: The instruction refers to the earlier July request for Japanese cannabis laws. It specifically asks about Ordinance No. 17, copies of which the Embassy had transmitted in August 1930.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3349 on Japanese cannabis laws
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Supplies Japanese legal information governing cannabis and other narcotics.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that neither the Embassy nor the Consulate General had received the cited 1937 diplomatic instruction. He encloses Mitani's statement that Japan had no special cannabis-import law and a translation of the relevant provisions of the 1930 narcotics ordinance as revised in 1934.

subfiles.title: Mitani letter on the absence of special cannabis laws
subfiles.from: Takanobu Mitani, Director of the Treaty Bureau
subfiles.to: J. F. McGurk, First Secretary, American Embassy in Japan
subfiles.about: Explains that cannabis importation is controlled under general narcotics rules rather than special cannabis legislation.
subfiles.summary: Mitani states that no special laws, ordinances, or regulations govern cannabis sativa in Japan Proper or other Japanese territories. Importation instead falls under the narcotics-control rules applicable in each territory.

subfiles.title: Translation of Japanese narcotics Ordinance No. 17
subfiles.to: Narcotics importers, exporters, carriers, and customs officials
subfiles.about: Sets out permit, documentation, transit, and reporting requirements for narcotics entering, moving through, or leaving Japan.
subfiles.summary: Articles 9 through 15 require permits for importing, transporting, exporting, or shipping narcotics and specify the information applicants must supply. Vessel captains and persons transshipping foreign narcotics must present export permits or transfer certificates to Customs. Permit holders must report completed movements and return unused permits; the ordinance was revised by Ordinance No. 33 in November 1934.

subfiles.title: Telegram requesting the alleged Saito letter
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Relays a Japanese request for a photostatic copy of a letter allegedly sent to Seiichi Amasaka by Mitsuji Saito.
subfiles.summary: Japanese authorities reported that Amasaka had arrived in Japan on October 29 after deportation following the Heian Maru narcotics case. They asked the Embassy to obtain the purported sympathetic letter from Saito that Amasaka said had been given to the federal court in Seattle. Grew also asked whether they could be told that the Department was investigating.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 3349 to the Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Forwards the Embassy's report and enclosures on Japanese cannabis controls.
subfiles.summary: The communication follows the Department's November 3 letter about the Marihuana Tax Act. It encloses duplicate copies of Despatch No. 3349 and its legal materials for the Commissioner of Narcotics.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment and renewed transmission of the 1937 cannabis inquiry
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Despatch No. 3349 and supplies the missing 1937 instruction on cannabis-import laws.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges receipt of the Embassy's October 18 despatch. It encloses two copies of Diplomatic Serial No. 2833 of September 9, 1937.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmittal of the Seattle investigation
subfiles.about: Sends Seattle Customs reports concerning the Japanese investigation of the 1937 Heian Maru morphine seizure.
subfiles.summary: Treasury forwards three copies of a November 28 report and its enclosures, together with a November 29 memorandum. The material investigates the purported Saito letter and the morphine hydrochloride seized at Seattle from the Heian Maru.

subfiles.title: Seattle Customs report on Amasaka and the Saito letter
subfiles.from: Green, Supervising Customs Agent at Seattle
subfiles.about: Reviews Amasaka's conviction, Nonaka's alleged role, and the discovery of the purported Saito letter.
subfiles.summary: The report states that Amasaka pleaded guilty and served a sentence for smuggling morphine from the Heian Maru. He had identified Nonaka as the scheme's instigator, while a notebook listed the soy-sauce containers holding the narcotics and an alleged agreement to support Amasaka's family if he went to prison. Customs found the previously unknown letter in the U.S. Attorney's files, supplied photostats, and noted that Shinji Taniguchi had been briefed on the case during his American visit.

subfiles.title: Customs Agent Bradt's memorandum on the purported Saito letter
subfiles.about: Evaluates the origin and likely purpose of the purported letter to Amasaka.
subfiles.summary: Bradt reports finding the letter in the Seattle U.S. Attorney's file but no information about when or how it arrived. Its Hammermill Bond watermark and English typescript led him to believe it was created in the United States, probably Seattle, and mailed from Japan to assist Amasaka's defense. Because Amasaka pleaded guilty, prosecutors had not pursued it further.

subfiles.title: Purported Mitsuji Saito confession letter and photostat cover
subfiles.about: Purports to absolve Amasaka while describing the concealment of morphine in soy-sauce containers shipped aboard the Heian Maru.
subfiles.summary: The writer claims sole responsibility and says Amasaka and Furuya Company knew nothing of the narcotics. He describes concealing morphine in five numbered containers among one hundred soy-sauce kegs, shipping them from Yokohama aboard the Heian Maru, and arranging for Chan to acquire them in Seattle. The accompanying page identifies the U.S. Customs Photograph Laboratory that produced the photostat.

subfiles.title: Request to Treasury for a photostat of the Saito letter
subfiles.about: Asks Treasury to obtain the letter sought by Japanese investigators of the Heian Maru case.
subfiles.summary: The State Department encloses a paraphrase of the Embassy's November 12 telegram about the Japanese investigation. It asks whether Treasury can provide a photostatic copy of the letter allegedly sent by Mitsuji Saito to Amasaka.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of the Embassy telegram concerning Amasaka
subfiles.about: Restates the Japanese request for the alleged Saito letter and permission to report that Washington was investigating.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase says Amasaka reached Japan on October 29 after deportation from the United States. Japanese authorities wanted a photostatic copy of the sympathetic letter allegedly placed with the federal court at Seattle and asked whether they could be told that the State Department was investigating.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the Japanese Geneva communiqué
subfiles.about: Points to a communiqué intended to rebut allegations against Japan concerning the opium trade.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references the Japanese Bureau's Geneva communiqué of September 30, 1938. It characterizes the document as an effort to answer accusations about Japanese involvement in opium traffic.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting the Seattle findings to Japan
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to give Japanese authorities the American findings about the purported Saito letter.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards the Treasury's December 10 letter and excerpts from its investigative enclosures. It asks that Japanese officials be shown Bradt's conclusion that the unsigned English letter was typewritten in the United States and that its author was unknown.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3460 reaffirming the cannabis-law response
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Explains that the Embassy had already answered the Department's renewed inquiry about Ordinance No. 17.
subfiles.summary: Grew refers to the November 3 instruction asking whether the 1930 ordinance remained in force. He notes that Despatch No. 3349 had already transmitted Mitani's statement and the pertinent parts of Ordinance No. 17 as revised in 1934.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about Japanese Army officers' anti-opium pamphlets
subfiles.about: Asks whether Japanese officers had published pamphlets condemning Army-protected narcotics and vice in China.
subfiles.summary: The Department encloses a November 29 New York Herald-Tribune editorial alleging that Japanese Army officers had protested the use of imperial authority to protect drug dealers and other criminal interests. It asks the Embassy to locate and translate any such pamphlets. The editorial writer recalled that the North China Daily News had mentioned them in 1935 or 1936 and that one was attributed to the Japanese general commanding the Tianjin garrison.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on representations over Japanese-sponsored opium accumulations
subfiles.about: Points to instructions for representations to Japan about large opium and opiate stocks accumulated in China through Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: The referenced material concerned the danger to the United States arising from major opium accumulations in China. It indicated that Grew was instructed to make representations to the Japanese Government.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of China Weekly Review excerpt on opium smuggling
subfiles.about: Forwards a press excerpt about opium smuggling from Sakhalin through Japan to China.
subfiles.summary: The State Department sends Treasury duplicate copies of an excerpt from the January 28 China Weekly Review. The article concerns the movement of opium from Japan to China.

subfiles.title: Japanese smash opium ring in Japan
subfiles.from: The China Weekly Review, citing Domei
subfiles.about: Reports the arrest of Chotaro Asada and associates for moving opium from Sakhalin through Japan toward Manchukuo and Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: Police at Kanazawa reportedly broke up a gang transporting opium from Sakhalin through Japan into Manchukuo and Tianjin. Alleged leader Chotaro Asada was said to have earned half a million yen before his arrest with two associates. The excerpt questions why opium was being exported to Manchukuo, already described as a surplus producer, and notes that Sakhalin had not previously been identified as an opium source.
